intro:
Lunch rush phone calls restaurant owners can manage best when the phone has a plan before the rush starts. The fix is not complicated: answer quickly, collect the right details, and send order calls to a system your kitchen can handle.

If you are short-staffed, a phone host can help cover the busiest stretch. ROAL can answer the phone, take pickup and delivery orders from your live menu, and send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen, while your team stays on food and service.

sections.h2: What should happen when the phone rings at noon?
sections.body:
At lunch, the phone should follow one simple path every time. That keeps the counter team from improvising while tickets are backing up.

Use this order:
1. Answer fast with the restaurant name.
2. Find out whether the caller wants pickup, delivery, hours, or a question.
3. If it is an order, collect items, sizes, modifiers, notes, name, and phone.
4. Give a ready time.
5. Repeat the order back.

A short script helps: "Thanks for calling Mario’s Deli. Are you ordering for pickup or delivery?" If the caller just needs hours or address, keep it short: "We are open until 3 today, and we’re at 18 Main Street." If someone asks about an allergy-sensitive item, catering, or a manager issue, hand it to staff with a quick summary.

For a busy lunch line, assign one person or one system to the phone. If nobody is available, route the call to [Rush-hour phone orders](/use-cases/rush-hour) or a phone host instead of letting it ring out.

sections.h2: Which calls should your staff handle, and which can be automated?
sections.body:
Not every lunch call needs a person at the counter. Separate the easy calls from the ones that need judgment.

| Call type | Best handling |
|---|---|
| Hours, address, parking, menu basics | Phone host or staff script |
| Pickup order | Phone host or trained staff |
| Delivery order | Phone host if you take phone delivery orders |
| Reservation request | Phone host can collect the request |
| Allergy-sensitive question | Staff with a summary |
| Complaint or manager request | Staff right away |
| Catering inquiry | Staff with details |

A phone host is most useful for repetitive lunch questions: "Are you open?" "What time do you close?" "Do you have chicken parm today?" ROAL reads the live menu and public pages during setup, so it can answer those common questions and take orders from what you actually sell.

Here is a practical rule: anything that needs a judgment call goes to a person, and anything repeatable can be handled by a phone host. That keeps your team from stopping a sandwich build just to answer the same five questions again.

sections.h2: How do you keep pickup orders accurate during the rush?
sections.body:
Accuracy matters most when the lunch line is moving fast. A missed size, modifier, or phone number turns into a problem at the window.

Use a tight order flow:
- Item name
- Size or quantity
- Modifier or note
- Caller name
- Callback number
- Ready time

A clear example sounds like this: "One turkey club, no tomato, add bacon, and one small soup, correct?" Then repeat it back before ending the call: "That is one turkey club, no tomato, add bacon, plus one small soup. Your name and number are John, 555-123-4567, ready in about 15 minutes." If the caller sounds rushed, slow the pace and keep the questions in the same order every time.

ROAL can do this kind of order capture from the restaurant’s live menu, then send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. It also does not take card numbers over the phone, so payment can stay the way your restaurant already does it. That matters during lunch because staff should not be juggling cash, food prep, and card entry at the same time.

sections.h2: What is the cheapest way to cover busy lunch calls?
sections.body:
The cheapest answer is usually the one that does not force you into a fixed monthly cost when orders are light. Many AI phone tools charge a monthly fee per location, whether the phone is busy or not. Human answering services usually bill per minute or per call. Delivery apps commonly take roughly 15-30% commission per order, which can add up fast on lunch tickets.

If you compare options, use your own numbers. Say you handle 40 lunch calls in a day, and 20 become completed orders. If your average order is $28, that is $560 in order volume. Plug that into your own math and compare it with a per-order model versus a monthly plan.

sections.h2: How do you set up forwarding before the lunch rush starts?
sections.body:
Phone forwarding is the backup plan when the front counter gets slammed. Many restaurants forward calls only when busy or unanswered, so the main number still works when staff can pick up.

A simple setup checklist:
1. Confirm your carrier or phone system instructions.
2. Decide whether to forward all calls or only busy/unanswered calls.
3. Test it with a real call.
4. Turn it off when you want the phone back on the desk.

On many landlines and some carriers, *72 then the forwarding number turns on forwarding and *73 turns it off. On some mobile carriers, **21*number# forwards all calls and ##21# turns it off. **61*number# can forward unanswered calls, and **67*number# can forward busy calls. Verizon Wireless uses *72/*73, and *71 for busy/no-answer forwarding. Business VoIP systems usually handle this in the web portal. Codes vary by carrier and plan, so always confirm and test.

ROAL can receive calls when you forward the restaurant’s existing number to it, and you can turn forwarding off any time. The restaurant keeps its own number.

sections.h2: What should your lunch-rush call script sound like?
sections.body:
A short script keeps the call moving and keeps the guest calm. You do not need a long greeting or a lot of small talk.

Try this structure:
- Greeting: "Thanks for calling Rosa’s Pizza."
- Purpose: "Pickup or delivery?"
- Order details: "What can I get started for you?"
- Close: "I have that ready in 20 minutes."

If the caller asks a question, answer only what helps the order. Example: "Yes, we have parking behind the building." If they ask about a menu item you do not carry, say it plainly: "We do not have that today, but I can tell you what’s similar." If the caller speaks another language, ROAL speaks the caller’s language on the call, which can help when lunch orders come in from a mixed neighborhood.

Keep a small checklist by the phone:
- Menu in front of staff
- Hours and address ready
- Pickup times you can realistically quote
- One person assigned to exceptions

sections.h2: How do you know the lunch phone plan is working?
sections.body:
You do not need a complicated dashboard to tell whether the plan is helping. You need a few practical signs you can check after the rush.

Look at:
- Missed or unanswered calls during lunch
- Which questions staff had to repeat
- Whether kitchen tickets were readable and complete
- Whether ready times were realistic
- Whether callers had to be called back for missing details

ROAL’s dashboard includes call history with transcripts and recordings, a kitchen screen with live tickets, a menu editor, hours, FAQs, upsell suggestions, and multi-location menus. That gives you a simple way to review what happened after the rush and tighten the wording or menu details if needed.

A useful weekly check is this: listen to three lunch calls, fix one confusing menu item, and update one hours or FAQ answer. That is enough to keep the phone smoother without turning it into a separate project. Built by Venkata Vamsi in Jersey City, ROAL is made for restaurants that need practical help, not extra work.

takeaways: Use one short script so lunch calls do not slow down the line.
Route simple questions, pickup orders, and delivery orders through a clear system.
Send allergy, complaint, catering, and manager requests to staff with a summary.
Compare fixed monthly phone costs with pay-per-completed-order pricing.
Test call forwarding before lunch starts and confirm it with your carrier.

faq.q: How do I stop lunch calls from interrupting my kitchen staff?
faq.a: Give the phone one clear workflow: answer quickly, take the order or question, and route exceptions to staff. If the front line is busy, forward unanswered or busy calls to an AI phone host or another backup number. That keeps staff focused on food instead of repeating hours and menu details.

faq.q: Should I forward all calls during lunch or only busy calls?
faq.a: Many owners prefer busy or unanswered forwarding so the restaurant can still answer when someone is free. Forward all calls only if the team is too short to handle the phone at all. Always test the setup with a real call, because carrier codes and phone systems vary.

It does not take card numbers over the phone, so payment stays with your usual process.

faq.q: What if the caller asks something the phone host cannot answer?
faq.a: Those questions go to an inbox, and the owner answers once. After that, the phone host knows the answer for future calls. For allergy-sensitive questions, complaints, catering, or manager requests, the host hands the call to staff with a summary.
